summary:
## Verdict

**Do not merge** — this change turns a strict origin allowlist into a credentialed CORS reflector for every caller.

## What broke

`corsHeaders` previously returned `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` + `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` only when `origin` was in `ALLOWED` (`https://app.example.com`). The new code always echoes the request `Origin` (or `*` when absent) and always pairs it with credentials.

**Failure mode:** any site the user visits can trigger a credentialed cross-origin request to this API (cookies / auth headers the browser attaches). Because ACAO mirrors the attacker's origin, the browser exposes the response body to that page — session data, account details, CSRF-sensitive mutations with readable results.

The PR framing (“native mobile clients / mobile webviews”) does not justify this:

- Pure native HTTP clients are not subject to browser CORS; loosening CORS does not help them.
- Webviews that do enforce CORS still need an explicit allowlist of known app origins (custom schemes, `https://app.example.com`, etc.), not “any Origin”.

## Secondary issue on the same path

When `origin` is `null`, the headers become `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` **and** `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. Per the Fetch/CORS spec that combination is invalid; browsers discard the CORS grant. So the null-origin path both fails open on security intent and fails closed for actual mobile clients that omit Origin.

## What to do instead

Keep an allowlist (env-driven if you need multiple webview origins). Only set ACAO to a concrete allowed origin; never `*`. Only set `Allow-Credentials: true` for those allowlisted origins. Native apps authenticate without CORS changes.

**Recommendation:** request-changes
